displayQuote: Never tell people how to do things. Tell them what to do and they will surprise you with their ingenuity

meta.title: Who really said "Never tell people how to do things. Tell them what to do and they will surprise you with their ingenuity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Patton: the line appears in his posthumous memoir War As I Knew It (1947), under "Issuing Orders." The "surprise you with their results" version is a paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never tell people how to do things. Tell them what to do and they will surprise you with their ingenuity'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Patton, from his memoir War As I Knew It (1947), in his advice on issuing orders. The popular "results" version is a later paraphrase.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Patton wrote it. The sentence appears word for word in his memoir War As I Knew It (Houghton Mifflin, 1947), in Part Three, “Reflections and Suggestions,” within his advice on issuing orders. We confirmed it in the book’s full text.

source.heading: Where the line appears

docMeta.dd: Part Three, “Reflections and Suggestions” — IV, “Command” — “Issuing Orders”
Bantam reprint (1980), whose printing note says it contains the complete text of the original hardcover edition

source.excerpt:
Commanders must remember that the issuance of an order, or the devising of a plan, is only about 5 per cent of the responsibility of command. The other ninety-five per cent is to insure, by personal observation, or through the interposing of staff officers, that the order is carried out. Orders must be issued early enough to permit time to disseminate them.

Never tell people how to do things. Tell them what to do and they will surprise you with their ingenuity.
trail: The memoir’s full text has the sentence under “Issuing Orders,” in section IV, “Command,” of “Reflections and Suggestions” (Internet Archive full text ↗).

The copy’s printing history gives “Houghton Mifflin edition first published November 1947,” with “Copyright 1947” held by Patton’s children (copyright page ↗). A library record lists the first edition as Boston, Houghton Mifflin, 1947 (Internet Archive catalog record ↗).
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced quotations, citing War As I Knew It (1947), “Reflections and Suggestions” (Wikiquote ↗). We found no Quote Investigator article on this quote.
source.excerptNote: The wording is the same as the popular version. Some quote collections, Wikiquote among them, put a comma after “what to do.” The text we checked has no comma there.

source.rightsNote: War As I Knew It was first published in 1947, and its copyright page records a renewal in 1975. Under U.S. law that keeps the book under copyright. Quoting this one sentence with attribution is ordinary fair use, but the book itself is not in the public domain.

author.name: George S. Patton
author.heading: About George S. Patton
author.metaLine: 1885–1945 · U.S. Army general, World War II
author.bio: George Smith Patton was born in San Gabriel, California, on 11 November 1885. He commanded American armies in North Africa, Sicily and Western Europe during the Second World War. He was badly hurt in a car accident in Germany and died in Heidelberg on 21 December 1945. His memoir, War As I Knew It, was published after his death, in 1947.

misattribution.heading: The popular paraphrase
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Patton is correct. A looser version of the line also circulates under his name, and that wording is not in the book.

items.who: “Don’t tell people how to do things, tell them what to do and let them surprise you with their results.”
items.why: This version was online by 2008. For example, a 9 April 2008 post on 37signals’ Signal v. Noise blog ↗ quotes it as Patton. Gracious Quotes says it has not found an original for this version and points to Patton’s actual wording in War As I Knew It (Gracious Quotes ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: What Patton actually wrote is “Never tell people how to do things. Tell them what to do and they will surprise you with their ingenuity.” It appears in War As I Knew It (1947) (full text ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is not a battlefield remark or a speech. It is a piece of written advice on command. Near the end of his memoir, in a part called “Reflections and Suggestions,” Patton set out lessons on soldiers, tactics and command. This sentence sits in his notes on issuing orders, alongside rules such as keeping Army orders to about a page and a half and issuing them early enough to be passed down.

Just before it, Patton says that issuing an order is “only about 5 per cent of the responsibility of command,” and that the rest is making sure the order is carried out. In that setting, the line separates what a commander must decide, the objective, from what he should leave to subordinates, the method.
context.pull: Tell them what to do and they will surprise you with their ingenuity.
